title: Early math: counting and number sense
purpose: Count, compare, add and subtract small numbers, and recognize shapes, patterns, length and time.
why: Counting and number sense are where every measurement of the brain and of behavior begins.
ready: Counts to 100, adds and subtracts within 20 using objects or drawings, and reads a clock to the half hour.

units.deliverable: Count objects at home to 20 and say which group has more.
Find five shapes around the house and sort objects by color and size.
Act out ten adding and taking-away stories with small objects.

topics: Numbers to 100 and counting by tens
units.deliverable: Week 7 check-up; build numbers to 100 with bundles of ten.
Solve story problems with drawings and number sentences.

topics: Telling time to the hour and half hour
units.deliverable: Measure toys with paper clips and read a clock at five times of day.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Make a counting and shapes book: a page for each number from 1 to 20, a shape hunt, and three story problems you made up.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

title: Math grades 2–3: place value, multiplication and fractions
purpose: Use place value to add and subtract within 1,000, understand multiplication and division, and begin fractions, area and data.
why: Place value and multiplication let you handle the large and small numbers of the nervous system: billions of neurons, thousandths of a second.
ready: Adds and subtracts three-digit numbers, knows multiplication facts to 10 × 10, and compares simple fractions.

units.deliverable: Add and subtract three-digit numbers two ways and check with the other operation.
Count coins, tell time to five minutes, and make a bar graph from a small survey.
Draw arrays for ten facts and find patterns in the 2s, 5s and 10s.
Week 7 check-up; write and solve equal-groups stories.

topics: Fractions as parts of a whole
units.deliverable: Fold paper strips into halves, thirds, fourths and eighths and compare them.
Find the area and perimeter of a room drawn on grid paper.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Run a pretend store: price items, add totals, make change, and record a week of sales in a bar graph.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

title: Math grades 4–5: multi-digit operations, fractions and decimals
purpose: Multiply and divide multi-digit numbers, add, subtract and multiply fractions, work with decimals, and measure angles, volume and the coordinate plane.
why: Fractions and decimals prepare you for rates, proportions and probabilities, the language of brain data.
ready: Divides multi-digit numbers, adds fractions with unlike denominators, and converts units within the metric system.

units.deliverable: Multiply and divide multi-digit numbers and check each answer by estimation.
List factor pairs up to 100 and generate equivalent fractions.
Solve fraction problems with models and with numbers.
Week 7 check-up; connect tenths and hundredths to money and metric units.
Convert the units in a recipe and find the volume of a box.
Measure angles with a protractor and plot a picture on a grid.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Plan a garden: use area, fractions of the plot, decimal costs and a coordinate map of where each plant goes.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

title: Reading foundations: letters, sounds and first books
purpose: Know every letter and its sounds, blend sounds into words, read sight words and simple sentences, and write first sentences.
why: Reading opens every book and article about how the brain works.
ready: Reads short decodable stories aloud, knows 50 sight words, and writes a sentence with a capital letter and a period.

units.deliverable: Name all 26 letters and say a sound for each.
Clap syllables and blend three sounds into short words.

topics: Letter teams: sh, ch, th and wh
units.deliverable: Read and spell 20 short-vowel words.

topics: Long vowels with a silent e
units.deliverable: Week 7 check-up; read 30 common sight words and silent-e words.
Read a short story aloud and name its characters and setting.
Retell a story in order and write two sentences about it.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Make a little book: write and draw a five-page story with a beginning, a middle and an end, then read it aloud to someone.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

title: Reading and writing grades 2–3
purpose: Read multisyllable words fluently, find main ideas and story structure, use text features, and write paragraphs, stories and opinions.
why: Clear reading and writing let you describe what you observe and explain why.
ready: Reads a grade-3 passage aloud smoothly, states its main idea with details, and writes a clear paragraph.

topics: Words with more than one syllable
units.deliverable: Decode 20 two-syllable words and sort them by vowel pattern.
Read a passage aloud at a steady pace and state its main idea.
Map a story's events and explain one cause and its effect.
Week 7 check-up; use headings, captions and context clues to answer questions.
Write a paragraph with a topic sentence, three details and an ending.
Write a short story and an opinion piece with reasons.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Write and illustrate a short nonfiction booklet about an animal, with headings, a glossary and a labeled picture.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

title: Reading and writing grades 4–5
purpose: Summarize and interpret literature and nonfiction, use word parts and grammar, and write informative essays, opinions and short research reports.
why: Explaining your reasons in writing is the start of every lab report and research paper.
ready: Summarizes an unseen text, supports an inference with evidence, and writes a five-paragraph essay that cites two sources.

reading.title: CommonLit: free reading passages for grades 3–12

units.deliverable: Summarize a story and support an inference with two quotations.

topics: Point of view and comparing texts
units.deliverable: Compare two accounts of the same event and explain similes and metaphors.

topics: Greek and Latin roots, prefixes and suffixes
units.deliverable: Identify text structures and decode words using roots, prefixes and suffixes.

topics: Grammar: parts of speech and agreement
units.deliverable: Week 7 check-up; edit a paragraph for grammar and punctuation.
Write a five-paragraph informative essay.
Research a question with two sources and present the findings.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Research report: choose a question about the human body, take notes from two sources, write a cited report and present it to your family.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

title: Science K–2: living things, weather and materials
purpose: Observe with the senses, sort living and nonliving things, care for a plant, watch weather and the sky, and test materials, pushes and pulls.
why: Living things and their senses are the first chapter of neuroscience.
ready: Describes an observation with drawings and words, and explains what plants and animals need to live.

units.deliverable: Observe five objects with your senses and sort things as living or nonliving.
Grow a bean seed and record its changes; match animals to their habitats.
Keep a one-week weather chart and draw the moon's shape each night you can see it.
Week 7 check-up; test which objects float and how pushes change motion.
Make sounds with vibrating objects and find land and water on a map.
Name body parts and their jobs; make a healthy-day chart.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Nature journal: observe one plant, the weather and one animal for two weeks, with a drawing and a sentence each day.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

title: Science grades 3–5: life, matter, energy and Earth
purpose: Explain life cycles, traits, ecosystems and adaptations, investigate matter, energy, forces, electricity and magnets, and model Earth, weather, space and the human body.
why: Science teaches you to test ideas against evidence, the core habit of brain science.
ready: Plans a fair test with one variable changed, records data in a table, and explains the result.

units.deliverable: Compare the life cycles of a plant, an insect and a mammal.
Draw a food web and explain how one animal's features help it survive.
Weigh water and salt before and after mixing, then separate them again.
Week 7 check-up; test how ramp height changes how far a toy car rolls.

topics: Weather, climate and the water cycle
units.deliverable: Model erosion with sand and water and explain the water cycle with a diagram.

topics: The solar system and Earth's motion
units.deliverable: Explain day, night and the seasons with a lamp and a ball, and trace a bite of food through the body.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Fair-test science fair project: ask a testable question, change one variable, record results in a table and a graph, and present your conclusion.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

title: Social studies K–5: communities, geography and early U.S. history
purpose: Understand communities, rules and citizenship, read maps, explain needs, wants and local government, and tell the story of early U.S. history from many perspectives.
why: People, communities and history are what the mind sciences try to understand.
ready: Reads a map with a key and compass rose, puts major events on a timeline, and explains how a law is made.

units.deliverable: Draw a map of your neighborhood and list the helpers who work there.
Label the continents and oceans and find three landforms on a map.
Make a simple budget for a class party and explain who makes local rules.
Week 7 check-up; compare how two Native nations lived in different regions.
Make a timeline from the first colonies to 1783.

topics: The Constitution and the Bill of Rights
A growing nation: expansion, the Civil War and civil rights (overview)
units.deliverable: Explain three rights in the Bill of Rights in your own words.
Finish the project with your grown-up; take the 30-minute final check in week 14.

project: Community history project: interview a family member or neighbor about how your town has changed, map the town, and make a timeline poster.
completion: finish the project with a grown-up, take the week 7 check-up and the week 14 final check, then redo any missed questions a week later. Show or tell one big idea from the course in your own words.

supplement.text: For government and citizenship, use Ben's Guide to the U.S. Government.
links: Ben's Guide to the U.S. Government

title: Computational thinking: instructions, patterns and algorithms
purpose: Follow and write exact step-by-step instructions, spot patterns, use loops and choices, find and fix bugs, break big jobs into small steps, and see how computers store information as numbers, all without a computer.
why: Step-by-step instructions and patterns are the seeds of algorithms and of models of the mind.
ready: Writes a short set of exact instructions that a partner can follow, shortens it with a loop, and finds the bug in a wrong set.

units.deliverable: Write instructions for a partner to draw a shape.
Shorten a long set of instructions with a loop.

topics: Breaking big jobs into small steps
units.deliverable: Find and fix the bug in three sets of instructions.
Week 7 midterm; sort ten cards by a rule and explain the rule.
Count from 0 to 31 with five binary cards.
Make a poster of three rules for staying safe online.
Submit the project; take an unseen 30 minute final in week 14.

project: Robot maze: draw a maze on grid paper, write step-by-step instructions with loops and if-then choices that guide a "robot" partner to the treasure, test them, fix the bugs, and present the final program.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: First programs in Python
purpose: Type and run real Python programs: print messages, do arithmetic, keep values in variables, repeat with loops, make choices with if and else, use lists, and write tiny functions.
why: Python is the main language of neuroscience data analysis and modeling, and you start writing it here.
ready: Writes and runs a five-line program that uses a variable, a loop and an if, and says what each line does.

reading.title: Raspberry Pi Foundation: free coding projects for young learners

units.deliverable: Print your name and a math fact.
Make a program that greets a friend by name.
Print a pattern of stars with a loop.
Week 7 midterm; write a program that answers yes or no.

topics: Lists: many things in a row
units.deliverable: Print every item on a shopping list.

topics: Putting it together: a tiny game
units.deliverable: Write a guessing game with a secret number.
Submit the project; take an unseen 30 minute final in week 14.

project: Story machine: write a program that tells a short story with variables for the characters, a loop for a repeated part, and if-else for two different endings; run it, fix any errors, and read the output aloud.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Math 6: ratios, rational numbers and expressions
purpose: Reason with ratios, rates and percents, divide fractions, use negative numbers and the coordinate plane, write expressions and equations, and summarize data.
why: Ratios and rates are how scientists describe firing rates, reaction times and accuracy.
ready: Solves ratio, percent and one-step equation problems and summarizes a data set with a center and a spread.

units.deliverable: Solve ratio-table and percent problems from real prices.
Divide fractions with models and the standard method; check with multiplication.
Plot points in all four quadrants and find distances on a grid.

topics: Expressions and the order of operations
units.deliverable: Week 7 midterm; write and solve equations for word problems.
Find the area of composite shapes and the surface area of a box from its net.
Make a dot plot and a box plot and describe the center and spread.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Survey project: ask a statistical question, collect 20 responses, display them two ways and summarize what they show.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Math 7: proportions, equations and probability
purpose: Analyze proportional relationships and percent change, compute with rational numbers, solve two-step equations and inequalities, and work with scale, circles, angles, volume and probability.
why: Equations and probability start the reasoning under uncertainty that brain and behavior research depends on.
ready: Solves multistep percent and proportion problems and computes simple and compound probabilities.

topics: Percent problems: tax, tips, discounts and percent change
units.deliverable: Identify the constant of proportionality from tables, graphs and equations.
Compute with negative fractions and decimals and explain the sign rules.
Solve and graph two-step equations and inequalities from word problems.
Week 7 midterm; make a scale drawing and compute a circular area.

topics: Surface area and volume of prisms
units.deliverable: Find missing angles and the volume of a prism-shaped container.
Run a simulation, compare it with the theoretical probability and judge a sample.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Scale floor plan of a room with its area, the cost of painting it with tax, and a probability game you design and test.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Math 8: pre-algebra, functions and geometry
purpose: Use exponents and scientific notation, solve multistep linear equations and systems, describe functions and slope, apply transformations and the Pythagorean theorem, and model bivariate data.
why: Functions describe how a neuron or a person turns an input into a response.
ready: Solves a linear system, finds slope from any representation, and uses the Pythagorean theorem in context.

units.deliverable: Compute with scientific notation using sizes from cells to stars.
Solve equations with variables on both sides and interpret a slope.
Solve one system by graphing, substitution and elimination.
Week 7 midterm; describe a function from a table, graph and rule.
Prove triangles similar and find distances with the Pythagorean theorem.

topics: Volume of cylinders, cones and spheres
units.deliverable: Fit a line to a scatter plot and use it to predict.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Model a real linear relationship, such as two phone plans, with a table, a graph and an equation, and decide which plan is better for whom.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: English language arts 6–8
purpose: Analyze theme, character, structure, point of view and arguments in literature and nonfiction, master grammar and vocabulary, and write narratives, explanations and evidence-based arguments.
why: Close reading and clear writing help you learn from articles and explain your findings.
ready: Writes an argument with a claim, cited evidence and a counterclaim, and analyzes an unseen passage.

reading.title: CommonLit: free reading passages for grades 3–12

units.deliverable: Trace how a character changes and state a theme with evidence.
Explain how structure and word choice create tone in two texts.
Judge whether a writer's evidence supports the claim.

topics: Grammar: phrases, clauses and sentence types
units.deliverable: Week 7 midterm; revise sentences for variety and correctness.
Write a narrative and an informative piece, each with a clear structure.
Write a cited argument and present it in three minutes.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Argument essay on a public-health question, such as later school start times, using three cited sources and answering a counterclaim.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

supplement.text: For writing and citation, use the Purdue Online Writing Lab.

title: Life science: cells, body systems, heredity and ecology
purpose: Explain cells and their parts, how cells build organ systems, how traits are inherited, how populations evolve, and how energy and matter move through ecosystems.
why: Cells, body systems and the nervous system are the foundations of neuroscience.
ready: Explains how a body system works from cells to organ, predicts a Punnett square, and reads an ecosystem diagram.

reading.title: CK-12 Life Science for Middle School

units.deliverable: Compare plant and animal cells in a labeled diagram.
Explain how cells, tissues, organs and systems are organized.

topics: The nervous, skeletal and muscular systems
units.deliverable: Trace oxygen from the air to a muscle cell.
Week 7 midterm; predict offspring ratios with Punnett squares.
Explain natural selection with an example and use a branching key.
Build an energy pyramid and propose one way to reduce a human impact.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Heart-rate investigation: measure resting pulse and pulse after one minute of jumping jacks for several willing family members, graph the results and explain the change.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Physical science: matter, motion, energy and electricity
purpose: Describe atoms, elements and the periodic table, distinguish physical and chemical changes, measure pH, and analyze motion, forces, energy, heat, waves, circuits and magnetism.
why: Electricity, motion and energy explain how neurons signal and how muscles move.
ready: Balances a simple reaction by counting atoms, computes speed and kinetic energy, and draws a working circuit.

reading.title: CK-12 Physical Science for Middle School

units.deliverable: Model three atoms and locate them on the periodic table.

topics: Chemical reactions and conservation of mass
units.deliverable: Show that mass is conserved in a sealed bag reaction of baking soda and vinegar.
Test household liquids with red-cabbage indicator and time a moving toy.
Week 7 midterm; explain a crash test with Newton's laws.
Compare insulators with cups of warm water and a thermometer.
Build series and parallel circuits with a battery and bulbs.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Kitchen chemistry and motion lab: rank household liquids by pH with red-cabbage indicator, and measure how ramp height changes a toy car's speed.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Earth and space science
purpose: Explain Earth's layers and plate tectonics, the rock and water cycles, weather, climate and natural hazards, and the motions of Earth, Moon, Sun and stars.
why: Earth and space science train the same habits of observation and measurement that brain science needs.
ready: Explains plate boundaries, reads a weather map, and models the phases of the Moon.

reading.title: CK-12 Earth Science for Middle School

units.deliverable: Label Earth's layers and the three kinds of plate boundary.

topics: Rocks, minerals and the rock cycle
units.deliverable: Draw the rock cycle with an example of each rock type.
Explain how a front produces rain on a weather map.
Week 7 midterm; compare climate and weather with data.
Make a family emergency plan and model eclipses and lunar phases.
Build a scale model of planetary distances.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Home weather station: record temperature, cloud cover and rainfall for two weeks, compare your records with the forecast, and explain the differences.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: History and geography 6–8
purpose: Use geography skills and primary sources to study ancient civilizations, world religions and empires, the medieval and early modern world, and U.S. history to industrialization.
why: History shows how ideas about the mind and the brain have changed over time.
ready: Analyzes a primary source for author, purpose and context, and writes a short argument from evidence.

topics: Early humans and the first civilizations
units.deliverable: Use latitude and longitude and explain why early cities grew near rivers.
Compare two ancient civilizations' governments and inventions.
Describe the beliefs and spread of three world religions in neutral terms.
Week 7 midterm; explain causes and effects of the Columbian Exchange, including disease.

topics: The American Revolution and the Constitution
The early republic and westward expansion
units.deliverable: Explain the main compromises of the Constitution.
Analyze a primary source from the Civil War or industrial era.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Primary-source project: analyze three primary sources about one period and write a short historical argument that uses them as evidence.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Programming in Python I: variables, decisions, loops and functions
purpose: Write Python programs that use variables, input and output, arithmetic, strings, decisions, while and for loops, functions and lists, and test and debug them by reading error messages.
why: Variables, decisions, loops and functions are the building blocks of every analysis and simulation of the brain.
ready: Writes a 30-line program with functions, loops and a list that solves a stated problem, and finds and fixes its own bugs from the error messages.

reading.title: Python for Everybody (free book and course)

units.deliverable: Write a unit-converter program.
Write a program that formats a name and an age.
Write a grade calculator.
Week 7 midterm; write a times-table printer.
Write and test three small functions.

topics: Putting it together: planning a program
units.deliverable: Write a program that analyzes a list of scores.
Submit the project; take an unseen 45 minute final in week 14.

project: Quiz game or text adventure: plan and write a 60–100 line program with at least three functions, a loop, a list and decisions; test it with a partner, fix the bugs they find, and write a short guide to how it works.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Algebra and functions
purpose: Manipulate expressions accurately, solve equations and interpret functions; these skills support every later calculation.

units.deliverable: Compute 20 mixed arithmetic examples and estimate answers first.
Solve equations with fractions and check each solution by substitution.
Solve one system graphically and algebraically; compare the results.
Midterm in week 7; repair errors and simplify mixed expressions.
Use at least two methods for a quadratic; state excluded values.
Model growth and explain domain, range and inverse operations.
Submit the project; take an unseen 90 minute final in week 14.

project: Build and explain a linear and an exponential model from a small invented data set.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major result aloud without notes.
why: Algebra and functions are the language of every model of neurons and behavior.
ready: Solves mixed unfamiliar algebra and function problems at about 85%, twice.

title: Geometry
purpose: Reason about angles, triangles, polygons and circles, prove congruence and similarity, use right-triangle trigonometry, and compute areas and volumes with coordinates and transformations.
why: Geometry describes the shapes, angles and spaces of the brain and of the visual world.
ready: Writes a two-column or paragraph proof, solves right triangles, and computes composite areas and volumes.

topics: Points, lines, angles and logical reasoning
units.deliverable: Write a short proof about angles formed by parallel lines.
Prove triangles congruent with SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS.
Find an unreachable height with similar triangles or a tangent ratio.
Week 7 midterm; prove properties of parallelograms.
Compute the area of a composite floor plan and the volume of a container.
Use slopes and distances to classify a figure on the coordinate plane.
Submit the project; take an unseen 60 minute final in week 14.

project: Design a garden or room with similar figures, right-triangle trigonometry and area and volume calculations, and justify every measurement in writing.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Trigonometry and vectors
purpose: Use radians, identities and vector components to describe rotations, geometry and oscillations.

units.deliverable: Draw the unit circle from memory and convert angular measures.
Sketch transformed sine and cosine functions and their domains.
Prove identities without circular reasoning; find all solutions in a stated interval.
Week 7 midterm; solve triangle and coordinate conversion problems.
Compute projections and explain orthogonality geometrically.
Connect complex phase to a real sinusoid; vary phase and amplitude.
Present the signal model; take an unseen 90 minute final.

project: Model a periodic signal with amplitude, phase and frequency; resolve two forces into components.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major result aloud without notes.
why: Trigonometry and vectors describe brain waves, oscillations and directions of movement.
ready: Derives identities and resolves 2D vectors unaided.

title: Precalculus
purpose: Choose and combine algebraic, graphical and trigonometric representations before starting calculus.

units.deliverable: Make a comparison sheet and solve unfamiliar composition problems.
Analyze zeros, multiplicities and asymptotes without a graphing tool first.
Estimate model parameters and check units and plausible ranges.
Week 7 midterm; work conics and coordinate geometry problems.
Derive arithmetic and geometric sum formulas and test simple cases.
Compute secant slopes and explain what a limiting process means.
Complete the portfolio and a 90 minute comprehensive test.

project: Analyze one rational and one trigonometric function with domain, intercepts, asymptotes and transformations.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major result aloud without notes.
why: Exponentials and logarithms describe membrane charging, forgetting curves and the senses' response to intensity.
ready: Completes a cumulative precalculus test in time, with clear written steps.

title: Calculus I
purpose: Interpret and calculate derivatives and integrals, connecting them to motion, optimization and accumulation.

units.deliverable: Work graphical and algebraic limits; identify discontinuities.
Derive a simple derivative from first principles.
Set up a related rates problem with a diagram and units.
Week 7 midterm; solve an optimization problem and justify extrema.
Interpret Riemann sums and compute signed area.
Explain why differentiation and integration are connected.
Deliver the motion analysis; complete a 120 minute final.

project: Model position, velocity and acceleration and recover displacement by integration.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major result aloud without notes.
why: Rates of change are how neuron models and learning rules are written.
ready: Passes a timed mixed exam; derives and interprets velocity and acceleration.

title: Statistics and probability
purpose: Describe and display data, use the normal model, fit regressions, design studies, apply probability, and make confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.
why: Statistics and probability are how every experiment on the brain and behavior is analyzed.
ready: Chooses and runs the right test for a question, and explains a confidence interval and a p-value correctly.

units.deliverable: Describe a distribution's shape, center, spread and outliers.
Use z-scores and fit and interpret a regression line.
Design a randomized experiment with a control group.
Week 7 midterm; compute binomial probabilities for a clinical scenario.
Construct and interpret a confidence interval for a proportion.
Test a claim and state the conclusion and its limits in plain words.
Submit the project; take an unseen 60 minute final in week 14.

project: Analyze a supplied health data set: describe it, fit a regression, test one hypothesis, and report the result with its uncertainty and limits.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.

title: Biology
purpose: Explain the chemistry of life, cell structure and transport, enzymes, respiration and photosynthesis, cell division, genetics, gene expression, evolution and ecology.
why: Biology, from cells to organisms, is the ground on which neuroscience is built.
ready: Explains respiration and protein synthesis step by step and solves dihybrid genetics problems.

units.deliverable: Classify biomolecules and compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
Predict osmosis in red blood cells placed in different solutions.
Track carbon and energy through respiration and photosynthesis.
Week 7 midterm; compare mitosis and meiosis and link cell-cycle errors to cancer.
